content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the class of models that use conditional computation as their building block. The authors claim that conditional models do not sometimes perform any better than non-conditional models and they hypothesize that this is because of the difficulty of estimating the gradients when using non-differentiable discrete routing. The authors experimentally compare multiple ways to estimate the gradients on various model and task families. The main finding is that an expert-designed routing is almost always better than a learned one. Additionally the authors experiment with labeling a small part of the dataset by expert-designed routing tags and find out that in this way the routing works as well as their expert-designed routing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

—-------------------

The paper has many strengths and is tackling an important problem. For the sake of time  I am only writing about weaknesses in this review, since those are the ones that should be actioned upon.

Weaknesses (W):

—-----------------------

W: One key reason for using conditional computation is to make inference less computationally complex in terms of FLOPS (often the amount of parameters is not as important as complexity during inference). One of the main flaws of the paper is that it does not specify in detail the networks that were used and whether they were matched in terms of parameters or computation. 

W: The DAE-Syn model was stopped at a certain iteration. Was this early stopping or was it after convergence? How was the model size determined in terms of potential under/overfitting, which may be different for conditional and unconditional models?

W: One key hypothesis in this paper is the lack of good estimation of the gradients. The authors compare 3 different methods, but the paper lacks any analytical comparison or even in-depth discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of these 3 methods.

W: How do the 3 methods perform with varying amounts of experts? How to choose good amount of experts?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writing clarity is good, but the quality, novelty and reproducibility could be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: In the current form, the paper is too incremental and lacks detailed comparison in order to justify publication.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The submission looks at conditional computation (CC) models and compares CC models with learned routing with models that use heuristics or non-learned algorithms for routing. The authors find the former under-performing against the latter on average and hypothesize that the used gradient estimation techniques are causal. By providing some amount of supervision (via attributes from part of the training set), this gap can be ameliorated.
Main contributions are experimental comparison between learned and non-learned CC methods, as well as sketching a possible solution that uses more supervision to help close the gap.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper provides a small, yet solid (multiple runs) experimental evaluation to make its point of a performance gap between learned and heuristic CC routing. The results of Section 4.1 demonstrate that in some configurations, learned routing may even not improve upon no routing at all (ST-Gumbel / Res-Dom).

The main weakness of the paper is the argumentation that the issue is with the approximate gradient estimation techniques themselves. This may very well be, but I don't see conclusive evidence for this hypothesis. Instead, the authors mainly manage to point out that more supervision (i.e., tag routing) is better than less supervision (e.g., any learned routing method in Table 1). The proposed methods in Sections 4.3, 4.4 basically just change the amount of supervision, as opposed to, say, improvements to any gradient estimation scheme, which leads to the not-very-surprising improvements. That said, it is encouraging to see that the amount of supervision provided can be on a small fraction of training data, at least in some cases.

A causal analysis would make the submission more convincing: are we really limited by the current gradient estimation approximations for routing, or is the amount of supervision provided the real cause of the improvements? This question is not explicitly answered, neither theoretically nor empirically.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The submission is overall clearly written and easy to follow. It introduces the methods used for learned routing (Section 2) and the experimental setup (Section 3) in self-contained fashion.
It is novel in the sense that it clearly compares various learned with non-learned routing strategies and shows that the common learned strategies still leave significant room for improvement. As discussed above, originality of the proposed solution is incremental.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I overall liked reading the evaluation of learned vs. non-learned routing strategies. As the authors mention, it is useful for "[setting] the stage for future work on conditional computation mechanisms."
The prominent claim that "these shortcomings stem from the gradient estimation techniques used" (cf. abstract), however, is not well supported by the experiments. Instead, the amount of supervision appears to matter the most. Thus I can recommend only with some reservations, unless the authors can significantly extend the discussion or theoretical evaluation provided.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper tries to answer the question: "Why do models with conditional computation learn suboptimal solutions?"
In essence, the paper has three experimental setups with different tasks to test conditional computation on, and shows that the baseline learning schemes everyone uses do not learn optimal solutions from scratch. These learning schemes do not seem to work well without a proper initialization, and in all scenarios underperform the simple heuristics significantly. However, as the paper shows, when initializing the blocks with sensible values, or with weak-supervision, the conditional computing methods can do well and outperform their monolithic counterparts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The question the paper raises is very interesting, and an important one
* The paper's experimental results are trustworthy, and make sense. 
* The conclusion that conditional computing learning methods do not work without initialization based on these experiments is an important one.

Weaknesses:
* The paper does not answer it's proposed question. It shows that indeed networks learn suboptimal solutions... but it doesn't show why. It does not even attempt this. There have been several papers on e.g. the difficulty of MoE training, I wished the paper would address any of these.
* The notion that any form of methods does not learn gates effectively by themselves, and that essentially initialization is important, was already known back in the old MoE days. Back when they were solved by EM algorithms, several papers already noted the importance of initialization. And although it's good that this work confirms that for newer gate training methods, it does not really tackle the underlying problem.
* I am missing quite a few key things and images for your story, that seem to have been relegated to the appendix. For example, the cover/focus results, the images that show me what the dataset you used for task 1 looks like etc.
* I am missing experimental details. These matter. For example, for the monolithic results, was the model size the same size as the others? Or just 'one block'?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is not entirely novel. The insight that MoE models are tough to train, and that with the commonly proposed techniques this doesn't necessarily work from scratch, is known. 
Based on the current form of the paper, without more extensive sections on the experimental setup, I couldn't reproduce the paper. However, it seems the authors will make their code available.

The paper is clear and well-written
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is in its current form the start of a research projects. Lab notes on the baselines wrapped into a paper. Starting of with the question "Why does conditional computing work sub-optimally", you would indeed start with showing that this is actually the case. However, for a full conference work, I believe the paper should go beyond that. Get into the 'why' of why conditional computing with these methods does not work very well. What is the underlying mechanism for the training methods to fail. Why does it then work if properly initialized? Show this with hypothesis, validated by experiments. Reference the literature that already tells us a thing or two about the difficulty of training MoEs. Look at pre-trained large-scale MoE architectures and verify that indeed these are suboptimal. 

Since the paper just shows results, and does not dive any deeper, nor does it introduce any real new insights apart from the verification that, yes, there is an issue, I have to reject this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper experimentally attempts to validate the claim that models with learned routers for conditional computation do not perform as well as models that use heuristic approximations for their routers.
By comparing 3 gradient-estimation routing algorithms to 3 heuristic routing algorithms, the authors suggest that the poor quality of gradient estimation algorithms is to blame for the suboptimal performance of learned conditional computation models.
They also show that the primary reason the learned routers don't perform optimally is that the learned routing is not very similar to the tag routing and that the performance can be increased if tag routing is used to supervise the learning process.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
- This paper is well-written and easy to read.
- The claims are clear and interesting.
- The experiments conducted are of high quality.
- The insight that you can use the tags to learn better routing is interesting and useful.

# Weaknesses
- It's not clear to me that the gradient estimation methods doesn't work.
Unless I'm mistaken, it seems like the tag routing heuristic uses auxiliary meta-information about the data that is not available to the other routers.
This means that the approach is unfairly biased in favor of the tag routing since it has access to more information than the learned methods.
For a fair experiment, I would like to see how the learned routers performed with the additional tag data provided along with the input.
It seems like the learned routers already do better than hash and baseline heuristic routers.
- It was a little hard to understand the DAE-Syn model; a figure would be very helpful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- This paper is well-written and extremely clear.
- The quality of this paper is high. The experiments are cogent and insightful.
- To my knowledge the results from this paper are novel.
- I did not attempt to reproduce the results in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper tackles an interesting problem and runs experiments that uncover some insightful properties about learned conditional computation blocks, I am not convinced of their claims based on their results. It's possible that I may have misinterpreted the paper in which case I would be happy to change my score, but currently, it seems like the tag-based heuristic, on which most of the paper is based, has extra information about the data not available to the learned routers. This seems like an unfair advantage, and it's not clear to me if the reason the gradient estimators perform suboptimally is that they are inherently unable to learn something patently clear from the data, or if they are just lacking the key piece of data that the tag heuristic is exploiting.
